meta.label: Vitamins and supplements
meta.attribution: Covers vitamin and mineral supplements sold in the US: multivitamins and single nutrients such as vitamin D, sold as tablets, softgels, capsules or gummies. Protein and sports nutrition, herbal and traditional remedies, probiotics, and children's supplements are separate decisions in this catalogue and are not covered here. This decision differs from Over-the-counter medicine in what it can honestly measure. OTC drugs go through FDA's monograph system and their labels are filed on DailyMed, so that lens can compare a safety warning printed on the label. Dietary supplements are regulated differently, under the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act: a company does not have to show FDA any evidence that a vitamin is safe or effective before selling it, and FDA does not approve the label first. So these scores never rate whether a supplement works or claim one brand is safer than another. They rate what can actually be checked about the seller: the price per tablet, softgel, capsule or gummy; whether the specific product was found in an independent tester's own public register, the USP Dietary Supplement Verified Mark or NSF Certified for Sport, both of which audit the factory and test the finished bottle rather than take the label's word for it; and how easy the product is to buy, a manufacturer's brand on many shelves against a single retailer's own store label against an online-only subscription. A product not found in either register is not proven unsafe or inaccurate, only unverified by the two registers checked here as of the search date given. The NHS states that most people get all the nutrients they need from a varied and balanced diet, included here as the free alternative to buying any of these. Not medical advice; a pharmacist or doctor can advise on individual deficiencies, pregnancy, or interactions with medicines. Reviewed 2026-08. Suggest changes via Contribute.

products.name: Varied diet, no supplement

economical.note: No product to buy, so no cost.

accessibility.note: NIH's Office of Dietary Supplements states that supplements can help a person get adequate essential nutrients if they do not already eat a nutritious variety of foods, implying that a person who does is already covered by diet alone. The NHS states this more directly: most people should get all the nutrients they need by having a varied and balanced diet, though it names specific groups, such as people who are vegan or who eat a limited diet, for whom a supplement can help.

links.label: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, what you need to know

products.description: Eating a varied, balanced diet, which the NHS says is enough to meet most people's nutrient needs without buying a supplement at all.
